A simplistic answer is that they are just reports of the items remembered from the input list. That answer does not suffice because we observe errors, that is, responses that do not correspond to items in the input list. A somewhat more sophisticated answer arising from a large body of research is embodied in what I will term the trial-unit nwdel, which constitutes a generalization of the familiar &amp;quot;modal model&amp;quot; of short-term memory (Baddeley, 1976; Mw-dock, 1961) and seems to be assumed implicitly by most investigators of short-term recall. This model, more aptly termed a framework for specific models, is illustrated in Figure 9.1."><meta name="citation_xml_url" content="https://api.taylorfrancis.com/content/chapters/edit/download?identifierName=doi&amp;identifierValue=10.4324/9780203772331-16&amp;type=chapterxml"><meta name="citation_inbook_title" content="Relating Theory and Data"><meta name="citation_firstpage" content="169"><meta name="citation_lastpage" content="188"></head>

in the most general terms, the question I wish to address is how to account for \nthe responses that occur in short-term recall. A simplistic answer is that they are \njust reports of the items remembered from the input list. That answer does not \nsuffice because we observe errors, that is, responses that do not correspond to items \nin the input list. A somewhat more sophisticated answer arising from a large body \nof research is embodied in what I will term the trial-unit nwdel, which constitutes \na generalization of the familiar &a;quot;modal model&a;quot; of short-term memory (Baddeley, \n1976; Mw-dock, 1961) and seems to be assumed implicitly by most investigators \nof short-term recall. A simplistic answer is that they are just reports of the items remembered from the input list. That answer does not suffice because we observe errors, that is, responses that do not correspond to items in the input list. A somewhat more sophisticated answer arising from a large body of research is embodied in what I will term the trial-unit nwdel, which constitutes a generalization of the familiar &amp;quot;modal model&amp;quot; of short-term memory (Baddeley, 1976; Mw-dock, 1961) and seems to be assumed implicitly by most investigators of short-term recall.
